title: Compare against the original Go beads and decide what to port
description:
Run one comparison round against the original Go `beads` (binary `bd`), reading
a local checkout supplied at execution time, and decide feature by feature what
is worth porting into this fork. Produce a decision document, not code.

This fork descends from `Dicklesworthstone/beads_rust`, a Rust port of the Go
original. The port is not complete, and the Go project has kept moving since it
was made — so this fork is missing two distinct things that need separating:
features the Rust port never carried, and features the Go project added
afterwards. This task tells them apart and picks the ones that matter.

## Baseline measured 2026-07-30

Go original (HEAD `750fd5741`, dated 2026-07-30 — actively
developed, merging PRs the same day):
- 1,881 `.go` files, ~573k lines.
- **191 distinct command tokens** registered via cobra `Use:` across
  `cmd/bd/*.go` (top-level plus subcommands).

This fork:
- **24 top-level commands** (plus `help`): blocked, close, comments, completions, config,
  create, delete, dep, epic, history, info, init, label, list, ready, reopen,
  search, show, stale, stats, status, sync, update, version (+ help).

The gap is not a to-do list. Much of the Go surface is deliberately out of scope
here: the Dolt storage backend, federation and peers, replicas and leases,
swarm/claim pools, db-proxy/server modes, and the issue-tracker bridges (jira,
linear, github, gitlab, notion, ado). The fork's whole premise is a local,
single-user, SQLite+JSONL tracker. Do not port scope back in by accident.

## What the round must produce

A written comparison, stored as an attachment on the epic this task spawns,
covering:

1. **A three-way classification of the Go command surface.** For each command:
   present here / absent-and-wanted / absent-and-deliberately-out-of-scope.
   State the reason for every out-of-scope call — "single-user local tracker"
   is a valid reason, "looks complicated" is not.

2. **The behaviour gaps inside commands we already have.** This is where the
   real value is, and a command-name diff will miss it entirely. Compare flags,
   output shape, and semantics for the 24 commands above — `bd show` vs
   `br show`, `bd list` filters vs `br list`, `bd sync` vs `br sync`,
   `bd epic` vs `br epic`. Note `bds-04l.9` already records that `br show`
   drops 9 fields in Rich mode; expect more of that class.

3. **Data-model deltas.** The Go `types.Issue` has fields this fork's `Issue`
   does not (the CHANGELOG's `LeaseGrantedNode` is one example, and it rides the
   JSONL interchange). Any field that travels in JSONL is a compatibility
   question, not a feature question: decide whether this fork must tolerate it
   on import even if it never writes it. `tests/storage_schema_shape.rs` pins
   this fork's serialized field set as a hard external invariant for `bv`, so
   any addition has to go through that test deliberately.

4. **A ranked port list** with one bead filed per accepted item, and an explicit
   rejected list. A comparison that ends in prose and no beads is a comparison
   nobody will act on.

## Constraints

- Read-only against that checkout. Never modify it, never build it into this
  tree, never copy Go source in.
- **Licensing:** the Go original is a separate codebase with its own terms.
  Porting *behaviour* and porting *code* are different acts. Check the Go original's `LICENSE`
  before any line-level borrowing, and record the finding in
  the comparison document — this fork's `NOTICE.md` already tracks lineage and
  will need an entry if anything is taken.
- The Go project is a moving target. Pin the comparison to the commit hash above
  so the document is falsifiable later.

## Sequencing

Do this after `bds-04l.5` (docs, agent surfaces, CI) and `bds-04l.8`
(GoReleaser). Those close out the fork; this opens the next phase. Running it
earlier means comparing against a surface that is still being stripped.

title: Version the JSONL format and give it a migration path
description:
The JSONL interchange format has no version marker and no upgrade path. That is
the real obstacle to changing the data model — not the database.

## Why the DB is not the problem

The SQLite side is already versioned and already migratable:
`CURRENT_SCHEMA_VERSION = 15` in `src/storage/schema.rs:10`, stamped into
`PRAGMA user_version`, with `run_pre_schema_migrations` (`:1185`) and
`run_migrations` (`:1315`) executing on open.

More to the point, `.beads/*.db` is **gitignored and derived** — see the
`.gitignore` that `br init` writes. `issues.jsonl` is the source of truth and
the database is a rebuildable cache. Changing a column is already close to free:
worst case, drop the DB and re-import.

So "add a way to change the DB model" is largely already true, and the honest
scope of this task is the format that *is* durable.

## Why JSONL is the problem

A record carries 14 keys — `id, title, description, status, priority,
issue_type, labels, created_at, created_by, updated_at, source_repo,
source_repo_path, compaction_level, original_size` — and **none of them is a
version**. `.beads/metadata.json` is two keys naming files. There is no place to
record which format generation a file was written in, so there is no way to
write an upgrade that runs once and knows it has run.

Two consequences, both live:

- **Adding a field is currently a breaking change with no ramp.**
  `tests/storage_schema_shape.rs` pins the serialized `Issue` field set as a
  hard external invariant because an external viewer parses the file directly.
  That test is correct and should stay strict — but strictness without a
  versioning story means the field set can never move.
- **Reading someone else's JSONL is all-or-nothing.** The Go original's records
  carry fields this fork does not model (see the parity round). Today the only
  options are "model it" or "drop it silently".

## What to build

1. **A format version, written once and read on import.** Decide where it
   lives: a per-record key, a header record, or `metadata.json`. A per-record
   key is the only one that survives concatenation and 3-way merge — this repo
   already ships merge-artifact handling (`beads.{base,left,right}.jsonl`) — but
   it is also the one the pinned field-set test will reject, so that test has to
   be part of the design, not a casualty of it.
2. **An upgrade path keyed on that version**, running on import, idempotent, and
   reporting what it changed. Model it on the existing DB migration gates
   (`user_version < N`), not on the probe-the-table style that sits beside them.
3. **A forward-compatibility rule for unknown keys.** Decide explicitly whether
   an unrecognized field is preserved on round-trip or dropped. Preserving it is
   what makes another tool's file safe to read and write back; dropping it is
   silent data loss and is what happens today by default. Whichever is chosen,
   pin it with a test that round-trips a record containing an unknown key.

## Prior art already in this tree — reuse it, do not reinvent

ID rewriting on import already exists and works: `br sync --rename-prefix` maps
mismatched IDs through `build_prefix_renames` (`src/sync/mod.rs:4515`), detects
collisions in `scan_import_collision_renames`, and applies the result inside
`stream_import_actions_in_tx` with foreign keys disabled and re-validated after.

That is the shape a data-level migration should take. Note what it demonstrates:
rewriting an ID is *not* a schema migration — it fans out into hierarchical
child IDs (which embed the parent ID verbatim), dependency rows, and free text.
Do not fold ID rewriting into the format-version mechanism; they are different
operations that happen to run at the same moment.

## Explicit non-goal

Do not build a general "rename any issue ID" command as part of this. Upstream's
Go implementation has `rename` and `rename-prefix` as first-class commands; let
the parity round (bds-i3g) decide on evidence whether this fork wants them.

## Acceptance criteria

- A JSONL file written by this version records its format generation, and an
  older file is recognized as older rather than assumed current.
- An import of a previous-generation file upgrades it, is idempotent on a second
  run, and says what it changed.
- The unknown-key rule is decided, documented, and pinned by a round-trip test.
- `tests/storage_schema_shape.rs` still pins a field set — the invariant is kept,
  with a deliberate, documented change, not weakened to accommodate this.
- `env -u RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN task check` exits 0, with every `running N tests`
  block paired to exactly one `test result:` line.

title: Render Markdown in the rich display paths
description:
`br show` prints every prose block as literal markdown source — `##` headings, `**bold**`, backticked code — because nothing in the tree renders markdown. `src/format/markdown.rs` is a complete but entirely unwired module; `rich_rust` is already a dependency with its `markdown` feature enabled. Wire it into the rich display paths only: styled markdown where styling is already permitted, byte-identical raw markdown when piped, under `--no-color`, or under `--json`, so `br show <id> | glow -` and agent parsing both keep working.

Architecture: a new `render_markdown_text(content, width) -> Text` in `src/format/markdown.rs` that splits the source into top-level blocks first, then renders each block knowing its kind — prose blocks wrapped here, fixed blocks (tables, fenced code, rules) rendered at exact width and left untouched. Consumed by `IssuePanel` and the two rich paths in `comments.rs`. The compact `format_issue_details` path is deliberately unchanged. The dead `src/format/rich.rs` is deleted rather than taught markdown.

Tech stack: Rust, `rich_rust` 0.2.2 (`markdown` feature, backed by pulldown-cmark), the existing `Text`/`Panel` renderables and `Theme`.
design:
# Render Markdown in the rich display paths

## The bug as reported

`br show` now prints every prose block — description, Design, Acceptance
Criteria, Notes — but prints them as literal markdown source: `##` headings,
`**bold**`, backticked code. The reported question was whether the main body
renders correctly and the other blocks do not.

It does not. **Nothing renders markdown anywhere.** Both display paths emit the
source text:

- `src/cli/commands/show.rs:1194-1237` — description, Design, Acceptance
  Criteria and Notes all pass through `wrap_body(sanitize_terminal_text(…))`,
  which strips control characters and soft-wraps on word boundaries. There is
  no markdown parsing in that path at all.
- `src/output/components/issue_panel.rs:93-100` — the Rich panel applies one
  flat `theme.issue_description` style to the whole description string.

## What already exists, and why it never worked

`src/format/markdown.rs` is a complete, unused module. It defines
`render_markdown` with Rich / Plain / JSON / Quiet behaviour, wrapping
`rich_rust`'s `Markdown` renderable, and `format/mod.rs:68` re-exports it.
**Nothing calls it.** `rich_rust` is already a dependency with the `markdown`
feature enabled (`Cargo.toml:97`), so the crate is in the tree.

This is not a regression. The module arrived unwired in the initial commit and
is equally unwired in the tree this project derives from (see `NOTICE.md`),
where `Markdown::new` likewise appears exactly once — inside the same dead
function — and `render_markdown` likewise has no callers outside its own unit
tests. There is no prior working implementation to restore or copy.

## Why wiring it up naively fails

`rich_rust`'s markdown renderer **styles but does not wrap**, and pads. Measured
directly against `rich_rust` 0.2.2 at width 80:

- A 210-column paragraph came back as a single 210-column line.
- A long list item came back at roughly 103 columns.
- Every *short* line is right-padded with spaces out to the target width.

Headings, emphasis, inline code, blockquotes, task-list checkboxes, GFM tables
and OSC-8 hyperlinks all render correctly. So what is available is a styler,
not a formatter.

That matters because `br show` gained soft-wrapping deliberately (`wrap_body`,
`show.rs:1050-1091`). Passing prose straight through the renderable would
regress it.

Two smaller findings from the same probe:

- Fenced code renders flat grey. `rich_rust`'s code-block path wants its
  `syntax` feature, which `Cargo.toml:94-97` deliberately excludes from the
  release build until the upstream syntect stack drops its unmaintained
  transitive crates.
- `markdown.rs:315` hard-codes `.hyperlinks(true)`, so OSC-8 emission is not
  gated the way colour is.

## Decision: piped output stays raw

Styled markdown is emitted **only where styling is already permitted**. Piped
output, `--no-color`, and `--json` keep byte-identical raw markdown.

This preserves `br show <id> | glow -`, which the agent-facing workflow
recommends, keeps agent parsing stable, and leaves the pinned goldens in
`tests/output_contracts.rs` untouched.

`show.rs:204` already splits exactly this way: Rich mode dispatches to
`IssuePanel`, everything else to the compact `format_issue_details`. **The
compact path therefore needs no changes whatsoever**, and the fact that
`tests/output_contracts.rs` stays green without modification is the cheapest
available proof that the decision held.

The same split holds in `comments.rs`: `:277` is the plain path and is left
alone; `:330` and `:384` are the rich paths.

Consequence worth stating explicitly rather than discovering later:
`br show --no-color` on a terminal resolves to Plain mode, so it too keeps raw
markdown.

## Approach: render per block, not per document

The flat `Vec<Segment>` that `Markdown::render` returns does not say which
output lines are a table row and which are a paragraph, and wrapping a table row
destroys it. Recovering that from styling alone is fragile.

Invert it: **split the source into top-level blocks first, then render each
block knowing its kind.**

New in `src/format/markdown.rs`:

```
render_markdown_text(content: &str, width: usize) -> Text
```

- **Prose blocks** — paragraph, heading, list, blockquote — render at `width`,
  then right-trim and wrap at `width` here, carrying a list item's leading
  indent onto its continuation lines the way `wrap_body` already does.
  Rendering at `width` loses nothing: `rich_rust` does not wrap, so an
  over-long paragraph comes back over-long either way, and the only effect of
  the width argument on prose is the right-padding that gets trimmed anyway.
- **Fixed blocks** — tables, fenced code, horizontal rules — render at exactly
  `width` and keep the renderer's own layout.

`rich_rust` does **not** clamp table width: a table asked for width 30 comes
back at 58 columns on every line. So `render_markdown_text` guarantees the
invariant itself — no emitted line exceeds `width`, with over-wide fixed-block
lines **cropped**. Cropping keeps a table row readable as a row; wrapping turns
it into mush, and an over-wide line breaks the panel border either way.

With that guarantee, the panel's existing `wrap_rich_text`
(`issue_panel.rs:271`) is a no-op on fixed blocks: it only touches over-long
lines. It can therefore stay in place unchanged, and the two wrapping layers do
not fight.

On any renderer error, fall back to the sanitized source text rather than
failing the command.

### The block split needs a parser, not a hand-rolled scanner

Add **`pulldown-cmark`** to `[dependencies]`. It is already in `Cargo.lock` at
0.13.3, pulled in by `rich_rust`'s `markdown` feature, so promoting it to a
direct dependency costs no new compilation — and it makes block classification
exact instead of guessed. The alternative is a hand-rolled markdown scanner,
which is the same fragility this approach exists to avoid.

Use it only to identify top-level blocks and their kinds, then slice the source
and hand each slice to `rich_rust`'s `Markdown::render`. Walking the full AST
and emitting `Text` directly is a larger design that was considered and set
aside; this is the narrow use.

**Caveat the split introduces:** rendering a block in isolation breaks
reference-style links, because `[text][ref]` and its `[ref]: url` definition are
different blocks. Either re-append collected link definitions to each rendered
block, or accept and document the limitation. Pin whichever is chosen with a
test.

### No wrapping crate

Wrapping stays in segment space, in this repo. `rich_rust`'s `Text::wrap` is
already style-preserving — it wraps via `slice()`, which re-maps spans onto the
sliced range (`text.rs:501-531`) — and is already used at
`issue_panel.rs:271`. The only thing it lacks is initial/subsequent indent, and
`wrap_body` (`show.rs:1050-1091`) already implements exactly that. Port that
logic from `&str` to `Text`.

A string-space wrapper such as `textwrap` cannot be used here even though it is
good at the job. `Text::cell_len` sums `unicode_width` per character with no
ANSI skipping (`cells.rs:27-38`): `ESC` measures 0, but the `[31m` after it
measures 4. Feeding a pre-rendered ANSI string back into a `Text` therefore
corrupts every downstream width calculation — panel borders, alignment and
wrapping alike. Every `&str`-in/`&str`-out wrapper forces that round trip.

## Ordering constraint

`sanitize_terminal_text` runs on the **source**, before rendering. The
renderer's own escapes are then the only ANSI present, and a crafted
description cannot inject its own.

Reversing this order would strip the escapes just generated *and* pass source
escapes through — a terminal-injection hole. Pin it with a test that feeds a
description containing a raw escape sequence and asserts it does not survive
into the output.

## Call sites

| Site | Change |
| --- | --- |
| `issue_panel.rs:93` plus the Design / Acceptance Criteria / Notes section and comments | `append_text(&render_markdown_text(…))` in place of `append_styled` |
| `comments.rs:330`, `comments.rs:384` | same |
| `issue_table.rs:279` | inline strip only — reuse the already-written `strip_markdown` (`markdown.rs:63`) |
| `src/format/rich.rs` | delete |
| `src/cli/commands/show.rs`, `comments.rs:277` | unchanged, deliberately |

`issue_table.rs:279` is the `--context` search-snippet cell. It gets stripping,
not styling: that cell's styling is owned by the search-term highlighter
(`highlight_text`), and a second styling pass would fight it. Block elements
cannot fit one table cell in any case.

## Deleting `src/format/rich.rs`

All six public items in that 540-line module have **zero users outside the
file**: `RichIssueTable`, `RichIssuePanel`, `RichDependencyTree`,
`format_status_badge`, `format_count_badges`, `build_completion_bar`. Each is
referenced only by the module's own two unit tests at `rich.rs:420,440`. The
module is kept compiling by nothing but itself, and is equally unused in the
tree this project derives from.

Teaching a dead second panel implementation to render markdown would be work
spent on code no command can reach. Delete the file and drop `pub mod rich;`
from `format/mod.rs`.

## Deliberately out of scope

- `src/format/syntax.rs` is also entirely unused — `highlight_code`,
  `parse_code_fence` and `detect_language_from_filename` have no callers. Leave
  it. It is the natural home for code-fence highlighting in a follow-up,
  precisely because `rich_rust`'s `syntax` feature is excluded from this build.
- `contains_markdown` and `escape_markdown` are unused; let them live or die
  with the implementation rather than making them a separate decision.
- `history.rs:726` prints diffs, and `error/structured.rs` prints error text.
  Neither is markdown.

## Testing

- Unit tests on `render_markdown_text`: a long paragraph wraps at width; a list
  continuation keeps its indent; a table row survives byte-identical; a fenced
  code block is preserved; no line carries trailing padding.
- A panel-level test asserting a rendered `## Heading` contains ANSI and no
  literal `##`.
- A regression test pinning `format_issue_details` output byte-identical to
  today.
- The terminal-injection test described under **Ordering constraint**.
- `tests/output_contracts.rs` must pass **unmodified**. Any edit to that file is
  a signal the piped-output decision was violated.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] `br show <id>` on a TTY renders headings, emphasis, inline code, lists, blockquotes, task-list checkboxes and GFM tables for description, Design, Acceptance Criteria and Notes — no literal `##` or `**` reaches the terminal.
- [ ] Comment bodies render the same way in `br comments` and inside the show panel.
- [ ] Long paragraphs and long list items wrap at the panel width; list continuations keep their indent; no prose line carries trailing padding (fixed blocks keep the renderer's own layout).
- [ ] Table rows, fenced code blocks and horizontal rules survive byte-identical — never re-wrapped.
- [ ] Piped output, `--no-color` and `--json` emit byte-identical raw markdown, unchanged from today.
- [ ] `tests/output_contracts.rs` passes unmodified — no edit to that file.
- [ ] `sanitize_terminal_text` runs on the source before rendering; a description containing a raw escape sequence cannot inject ANSI into the output, pinned by a test.
- [ ] A renderer error falls back to the sanitized source text rather than failing the command.
- [ ] `src/format/rich.rs` is deleted and `pub mod rich;` removed from `format/mod.rs`.
- [ ] `env -u RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN task check` exits 0.
notes:
# Global Constraints

Every task's requirements implicitly include this section.

## Toolchain

- **Prefix every `cargo` / `rustc` / `task` invocation with `env -u RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN`.** There is no `rust-toolchain.toml`; a stale exported `RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN` silently builds on nightly and still reports success.
- The gate is `env -u RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN task check` and it must exit 0 before any commit. It runs `toolchain:check`, `format:check`, `lint` (clippy over every target), then `test`.
- `rust-version = "1.95"`. Do not use features newer than that.
- Building needs a C compiler — `rusqlite`'s `bundled` feature compiles SQLite from C source.

## Tests

- The suite runs under **cargo-nextest**, one process per test. `task test` runs `cargo nextest run --workspace --no-fail-fast` **and then** `cargo test --workspace --doc`. Never substitute a bare `cargo nextest run` — nextest cannot run doctests and they would silently stop running.
- Run a subset with `env -u RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN task test:one -- -E 'test(<name>)'`. Nextest selects by filterset, not `--test <binary> <name>`.
- Clippy runs with **pedantic + nursery** (`[lints.clippy]` in `Cargo.toml`). New code must pass without `#[allow]` unless an existing neighbouring pattern already uses one.
- Do not reconcile test counts by arithmetic. Use `cargo nextest list --workspace` before and after and diff the actual names.

## Files that must not change

- **`tests/output_contracts.rs` must pass unmodified.** Any edit to that file means the piped-output decision was violated. It pins the machine-readable goldens consumers parse.
- The compact path `format_issue_details` (`src/cli/commands/show.rs:1094-1282`) and the plain comments path (`src/cli/commands/comments.rs:277`) stay byte-identical. Piped output, `--no-color` and `--json` keep raw markdown.

## Where a new test goes

- Unit tests live in a `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` inside the module under test. That is where every test in this plan goes.
- Integration tests are grouped into a handful of binaries; a new file needs both a file in the directory **and** a `#[path]` line in the crate root (`tests/e2e.rs`, `tests/storage.rs`, `tests/proptest.rs`, `tests/repro.rs`). No task in this plan adds one.

## Licensing guard

- `tests/licensing.rs` fails the build if any git-tracked file other than `NOTICE.md` and itself names an upstream project or a path on someone else's machine. Do not write such a sentence in a doc comment, a README section, or a commit message that ends up quoted in a tracked file. Link to `NOTICE.md` instead.
- Never describe this project as plain-MIT-licensed. `Cargo.toml` uses `license-file` because the licence carries a binding rider with no SPDX identifier.
- After staging any new or edited tracked file, run `env -u RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN cargo test --test licensing`.

## Commits

- **Commit messages must parse as Conventional Commits.** `.cliff.toml` builds `CHANGELOG.md` from them and that becomes the release body. Accepted: `feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `chore`, `build`, `ci`, `test`, `perf`, `style`, `refactor`, `revert`, plus a `!` breaking marker. `plan:` is rejected.
- **Never add AI or agent attribution trailers** — no `Co-Authored-By` naming an assistant, no `Generated with …`, no variant, in any commit, PR body, release note or tag message. Nothing in the gate or the hooks will catch one, and history is not rewritable once pushed.
- Do not skip hooks and do not add `--no-verify`. Install them once with `pre-commit install`.

## The remote

- **Never write to the remote without explicit approval, every time.** No `git push` in any form, no `gh pr` / `gh release` / `gh workflow run`, no `gh api` with a non-GET method, no tag push.
- Reading is fine and needs no approval: `gh pr list`, `gh pr diff`, `gh run view`, `gh api` GETs.
- Local work — committing, branching, resetting — is outside this rule.

title: Wire markdown rendering into IssuePanel
description:
Consume `render_markdown_text` in `src/output/components/issue_panel.rs`, replacing `append_styled` with `append_text` for every prose block: the description (:93-100), the Design / Acceptance Criteria / Notes section, and comment bodies (:262-266).

# Task 7: Strip markdown from the `--context` search snippet

**Depends on Task 4** only for `strip_markdown` being `pub(crate)`. Independent
of Tasks 5 and 6.

**Files:**
- Modify: `src/output/components/issue_table.rs:275-285` — the `--context` cell
- Modify: `src/format/markdown.rs` — export `strip_markdown` as `pub(crate)`, drop the `#[allow(dead_code)]` Task 4 left on it
- Modify: `src/output/components/issue_table.rs:338` (`mod tests`) — add one test

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: `crate::format::markdown::strip_markdown(content: &str) -> String`
- Produces: `fn plain_snippet(snippet: &str) -> String` — private to `issue_table.rs`

## Why stripping and not styling

This cell is the search-context snippet. Two reasons it must not be styled:

1. The cell's styling is already owned by the query highlighter — the existing
   `highlight_text(sanitized_snippet, highlight_regex, theme)` call immediately
   below. A second styling pass would fight it.
2. Block elements cannot fit in one table cell in any case.

So the goal is only that a snippet reads as clean prose instead of showing `##`
and `**` markers.

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**

Add to `mod tests` in `src/output/components/issue_table.rs`:

```rust
#[test]
fn plain_snippet_strips_markers_and_flattens_to_one_line() {
    let snippet = "## Heading\n\nSome **bold** and `code` text.";
    let out = plain_snippet(snippet);

    assert!(!out.contains('#'), "got {out:?}");
    assert!(!out.contains('*'), "got {out:?}");
    assert!(!out.contains('\n'), "a table cell must be one line: {out:?}");
    assert!(out.contains("Heading"));
    assert!(out.contains("bold"));
}

#[test]
fn plain_snippet_sanitizes_terminal_escapes() {
    let out = plain_snippet("danger \x1b[2J here");
    assert!(!out.contains('\x1b'), "raw escape survived: {out:?}");
}
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run it to make sure it fails**

```bash
env -u RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN task test:one -- -E 'test(plain_snippet)'
```

Expected: FAIL — compile error, `cannot find function plain_snippet`.

- [ ] **Step 3: Make `strip_markdown` visible**

In `src/format/markdown.rs`, change:

```rust
fn strip_markdown(content: &str) -> String {
```

to:

```rust
pub(crate) fn strip_markdown(content: &str) -> String {
```

and delete the `#[allow(dead_code)]` Task 4 attached to it.

- [ ] **Step 4: Write the implementation**

In `src/output/components/issue_table.rs`:

```rust
/// Flatten a search snippet for a one-line table cell.
///
/// Stripped rather than rendered: this cell's styling belongs to the query
/// highlighter applied just after, and block elements cannot fit one cell.
fn plain_snippet(snippet: &str) -> String {
    let sanitized = sanitize_terminal_text(snippet);
    crate::format::markdown::strip_markdown(sanitized.as_ref())
        .split_whitespace()
        .collect::<Vec<_>>()
        .join(" ")
}
```

`split_whitespace().join(" ")` is what collapses the newlines `strip_markdown`
leaves behind into the single line a table cell needs.

Then replace the cell construction (currently `:275-285`):

```rust
if self.columns.context {
    let snippet = self
        .context_snippets
        .as_ref()
        .and_then(|snippets| snippets.get(&issue.id))

    let snippet_text = highlight_text(&plain, highlight_regex.as_ref(), self.theme);
    cells.push(Cell::new(snippet_text).style(self.theme.muted.clone()));
}
```

The `sanitize_terminal_text` call moves inside `plain_snippet`, so remove the

title: Over-wide markdown tables crop to near-nothing in br show
description:
Symptom: in a 100-column terminal, `br show bds-jgk` renders the Call-sites table with the first column at ~86 columns and the second cropped to five characters ("Chang", "appe", "same"). The row structure survives but the content does not.

Repro: `br show bds-jgk` on a 100-column TTY, scroll to the 'Call sites' table in the Design field.

Cause: rich_rust lays a table out at its natural content width and does not clamp to the requested width — a table asked for width 30 comes back at 58. bds-jgk.1.3 added crop-to-width for fixed blocks so an over-wide line cannot break the panel border or be shredded by wrap_rich_text. Cropping preserves row structure, which is why it was chosen over wrapping, but for a table whose natural width far exceeds the panel it discards most of the content.

Expected: an over-wide table should remain readable. Two candidate approaches, neither yet chosen:
1. Fall back to emitting the table's raw markdown source as prose when its rendered width exceeds the target, so every cell is visible and wraps normally. Loses the box drawing, keeps the content.
2. Pre-narrow the table before handing it to rich_rust, or post-process column widths.

Also observed while investigating: inline code inside a table cell is NOT rendered — `issue_panel.rs:93` keeps its literal backticks. That is a rich_rust table-cell limitation, separate from the width problem.

Not a regression: before this epic the whole body printed as raw markdown, so nothing that used to be readable became unreadable. This is a shortfall of the new rendering, not a step backwards.

comments.author: anton
comments.text: Fixed in c4beec4. Rather than either candidate in the description, tables now render through rich_rust's Table renderable, whose render(max_width) is a true maximum: it wraps cell content to fit and leaves a narrower table at its natural size. So the box drawing AND the content both survive. Verified on the original repro (br show bds-jgk at 100 columns): the Call-sites second column is fully readable. The inline-code observation is also fixed incidentally -- cells are flattened from the parser's events, so an Event::Code contributes its text without backticks.

title: Nested fixed blocks are classified as Prose and get shredded
description:
Symptom: a fenced code block inside a list item, or a table inside a blockquote, is wrapped as prose instead of being left alone. Confirmed live on a 40-column pty: a code line inside a numbered list wrapped across three lines, and a blockquoted table came out as `| column alpha | column beta |` / `column gamma |` — exactly the row-shredding the Fixed/crop design exists to prevent.

Cause: `classify_block` (src/format/markdown.rs:80) inspects only the TOP-LEVEL tag. `split_top_level_blocks` emits one block per top-level element, so a List or BlockQuote containing a CodeBlock or Table is classified Prose in its entirety and routed through `wrap_text_with_indent`.

Expected: a fixed sub-element should keep the renderer's layout wherever it appears. Likely needs the splitter to descend into container blocks and emit mixed Prose/Fixed segments, rather than classifying the container as a whole.

Not a regression — before this epic the entire body printed as literal markdown. And 0 of 26 prose fields in this repo's own .beads/issues.jsonl hit it today. But code blocks inside list items are very common markdown, and the corruption is silent.

No test covers nesting: split_top_level_blocks_classifies_each_block asserts top-level only, and split_top_level_blocks_keeps_nested_lists_as_one_block asserts the grouping without exercising its consequence. Any fix must add one.

Found by the epic's final whole-branch review.

comments.author: anton
comments.text: Fixed in c4beec4. split_blocks now descends into containers and lifts each code block and table out, rather than classifying the container whole. Their content comes from the parser's events, not a source slice: pulldown-cmark strips a container's prefix from the nested block's first line only, so the range of a fence inside a blockquote still carries '> ' on every following line. Prose keeps its source slice, so a list's numbering survives the split (rich_rust honours an ordered list's start number). Three tests added at the splitter and two end-to-end, per the note that no test covered nesting. One thing changed beyond the report: lifting nested code out meant it would now be cropped like top-level code, losing content the prose path had preserved, so code lines are broken at the width boundary instead -- every character survives.

title: br hangs forever after its terminal hangs up, holding the write lock
description:
Symptom: `br` never exits and holds `.beads/.write.lock`, so every later `br`
in that repo fails with "Timed out ... waiting for write lock". Observed live:
a `br search needle` process still running 2h09m after its terminal was gone.

Trigger: the controlling terminal hangs up (terminal window closed, ssh drop,
tmux kill-session) while a `br` command is running. Any of the three
`terminal_width()` callers is enough -- `br list`, `br search`, `br ready`.

Root cause: an interaction between two deliberate choices, neither wrong alone.

1. `shutdown::install()` (src/shutdown.rs) handles SIGHUP so a hangup unwinds
   the stack and lets SqliteStorage::Drop flush the WAL (#270). `br` therefore
   SURVIVES a hangup that would kill an ordinary process.
2. `format::text::terminal_width()` calls `crossterm::terminal::size()`, whose
   unix path does `File::open("/dev/tty")` before falling back to
   STDOUT_FILENO. On a hung-up controlling terminal that open never returns.
   crossterm's fallback only fires when the open *fails*, and a blocking open
   never fails.

Stack, from `sample` on the live process and reproduced identically:

    beads::format::text::terminal_width
      -> crossterm::terminal::sys::unix::window_size
        -> std::fs::OpenOptions::__open
          -> __open  (in libsystem_kernel.dylib)   <- blocks forever

Isolation: same pty, same hangup, same probe; the only variable is SIGHUP
handling. Default disposition -> the process dies before reaching the open.
Handler installed -> it survives, reaches the open, and blocks.

Repro (macOS; the window is wide relative to br's runtime, 1 hang in 2-3 tries):
fork a pty, exec `br search <term>` in the child, close the master after a
jittered 0.5-30ms, then check whether the child is still alive. A driver
script is in the fix commit's message trail; the essential steps are above.

Severity measured, not assumed: with one hung process present,
`br --lock-timeout 10000 create "x"` in the same repo timed out after 10s.

Fix: never open /dev/tty to measure width. Query the winsize on a descriptor
already held (stdout, then stderr, then stdin) via rustix::termios::tcgetwinsize,
which is safe (`unsafe_code = "forbid"` rules out a hand-rolled ioctl) and
already in Cargo.lock via crossterm's own non-libc path.

Note this is arguably a crossterm bug too, but beads can fix it locally.

comments.author: anton
comments.text: Fixed. The first fix was incomplete and the verification caught it: replacing crossterm::terminal::size() in format::text::terminal_width() left the hang fully intact, because rich_rust reaches the same blocking open independently -- Console::print_renderable -> Console::options -> Console::width() -> rich_rust::terminal::get_terminal_width() -> crossterm::terminal::size(). A Console resolves its size lazily, so every rich render probed the terminal. Two fixes were needed: (1) terminal_width/terminal_height read the winsize from stdout/stderr/stdin via rustix::termios::tcgetwinsize, opening nothing; (2) all 30 Console construction sites now go through crate::output::console(), which pins width and height up front so rich_rust never probes. ConsoleBuilder::build starts from Console::new() and overrides only what is set, so rendering is otherwise unchanged. Verified: 0 hangs in 300 races for br search and 120 each for list/ready/stats, against 1 hang within 2-3 races before. Two source guards in tests/repro/tty_hangup_width.rs, both confirmed to fail when violated. An automated hang test is not possible here: giving a child a controlling terminal needs setsid + TIOCSCTTY via Command::pre_exec, which unsafe_code = forbid rules out.

title: Nothing in the build can see dead public code
description:
`cargo check --workspace --all-targets` exits 0 with **zero warnings**, and yet a
sweep of the tree finds roughly forty unreferenced `pub` functions, four
unreferenced `clap` argument structs, and an entire storage submodule whose
writer half nothing calls. None of that is a lint bug. It is a structural
consequence of how the crate is shaped, and until the shape changes no amount
of care at review time will keep the number from growing again.

## Why the lint is blind

`src/lib.rs` declares every module `pub`:

```
pub mod cli;      pub mod close_policy;  pub mod config;
pub mod error;    pub mod format;        pub mod health;
pub mod inheritance;                     pub mod logging;
pub mod model;    pub mod output;        pub mod shutdown;
pub mod storage;  pub mod sync;          pub mod util;
pub mod validation;
```

`dead_code` fires only on items rustc can prove are unreachable *from outside
the crate too*. A `pub fn` in a `pub mod` of a `lib` target is reachable by
definition — some hypothetical downstream crate might call it — so the lint
declines to fire, correctly, and stays silent forever.

The catch is that the hypothesis is false here. `Cargo.toml` sets
`publish = false`; there is exactly one consumer of this library, the `br`
binary in the same package, plus the integration tests. Every `pub` in this
tree is `pub(crate)` in practice while being `pub` to the compiler, and the
gap between those two facts is precisely the space the dead code lives in.

Note what this is *not*: it is not an argument that the modules should be
private. The integration tests under `tests/` link the library and reach into
`beads::storage`, `beads::sync`, `beads::config` and friends directly; that is
the point of having a lib target at all. The visibility is load-bearing. What
is missing is a check that distinguishes "reachable from the binary or a test"
from "reachable in principle."

## Why this is worth fixing rather than living with

The sweep that produced the sibling issues in this batch was ad-hoc: extract
every `pub fn` name, count identifier occurrences across `src/`, `tests/` and
`test-support/`, and treat "occurs exactly as many times as it is defined" as
dead. That works, and it caught real things, but it has at least one known
blind spot — a thin wrapper that forwards to an identically-named inner
function inflates both counts, so the pair looks used while both halves are
unreachable. Two confirmed instances got past the first pass that way
(`SqliteStorage::get_all_events` / `events::get_all_events`, and
`events::count_events`). A one-off script is not a gate, and the next review
starts from scratch.

## Options, roughly in increasing order of intrusiveness

1. **Run something that already knows how to do this.** `cargo-udeps` solves a
   different problem (unused *dependencies*); the relevant tools here are
   `warnalyzer` or a `rust-analyzer`-driven pass, both of which resolve
   references properly rather than counting identifiers. Wire one into
   `task check`, or into a non-blocking `task lint:dead` that CI reports.
2. **Make the binary the only public surface.** Downgrade `pub mod` to
   `pub(crate) mod` and re-export a deliberate façade for the tests. Then
   `dead_code` fires on its own, no new tooling, and it fires *at compile time
   for the person who wrote the code*. The cost is churn in `tests/` and a
   real design decision about what the tested surface is.
3. **Split the crate.** A `beads-core` lib with a genuinely public API and a
   `br` bin that depends on it. Most faithful to the actual architecture,
   largest change, and probably not worth it on its own — but it is the option
   the other two approximate.

Option 1 is the cheapest thing that would have caught every item in this batch
and would keep catching them. Option 2 is the one that makes the problem stop
existing. They are not exclusive.

## Acceptance criteria

- A repeatable command reports unreferenced `pub` items in `src/`, and running
  it on the tree as it stands reproduces the sibling findings in this batch
  rather than a subset of them.
- Whatever is chosen is wired into the repository's own workflow (`Taskfile.yml`
  and/or CI) so it runs without anyone remembering to run it, and `CLAUDE.md`
  says which command it is.
- If the check is advisory rather than blocking, that is stated deliberately in
  `CLAUDE.md` alongside the existing note about `task test:report` being a
  diagnostic and not a gate — the distinction already has a precedent there.
- The wrapper-pair blind spot described above is covered: a test or a
  self-check demonstrates the chosen tool flags
  `SqliteStorage::get_all_events` (`src/storage/sqlite.rs:1955`).
- `env -u RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN task check` exits 0.

comments.text:
Diagnostic pass done (this bead's step 1). The gate is deliberately not landed
yet. Method and authoritative list recorded here so nobody redoes it.

Method: a throwaway edit to src/lib.rs -- every `pub mod` to `pub(crate) mod`,
plus `extern crate self as beads;` and `#[path = "main.rs"] pub mod bin_root;`
so the binary compiles as part of the library. That is option 2 from this
bead, run as a measurement rather than landed.

One correction that matters if you repeat it: `fn main` is private, so with
the visibility change alone rustc has no roots at all and reports the entire
crate dead -- 1669 warnings. Making it `pub fn main` gives the real answer:
109 dead_code diagnostics covering 222 distinct items.

Because rustc's analysis is reachability from roots rather than occurrence
counting, it has none of the ad-hoc sweep's blind spots -- the wrapper pair
this bead calls out is reported as a whole cluster.

Classifying the 222 by who still references them:

     76  referenced NOWHERE -- not from main, not from any test
     76  referenced only by #[cfg(test)] blocks inside src/
     70  referenced by tests/ or test-support/

The middle bucket is the one the ad-hoc sweep could not have found, and the
most interesting: dead product code that still has passing unit tests
attached. The tests keep it compiling and give it the appearance of being
maintained.

By file, the 76 that nothing references at all: storage/sqlite.rs 27,
health.rs 11, error/structured.rs 6, util/id.rs 6, config/mod.rs 4,
format/syntax.rs 4, output/components/issue_panel.rs 3, then a tail of 1-2
across cli/mod.rs, storage/conn.rs, sync/mod.rs, output/context.rs and others.

Caveat: #[cfg(test)] regions were detected by brace balance, which is
approximate. Treat the 76/76 split as having a small error bar; the 222 total
and the reachability result are exact.

Two consumers already: bds-y6o (closed -- every item it named appears in this
list, which was its own acceptance criterion) and bds-cn6, which should be
re-scoped to these 152 rather than its original inventory.

The gate should land after the deletions, not before, or it fails on arrival.

comments.text:
Deferred to last, deliberately, and dropped to P3.

The diagnostic half of this bead has been run four times now (see the
comment above and bds-cn6), and each run is cheap: patch src/lib.rs to
pub(crate), make `fn main` pub, `cargo check --lib`, revert. What is missing
is the ratchet -- a repeatable command wired into the Taskfile, documented in
CLAUDE.md, with the advisory-vs-blocking question answered.

Landing that ratchet before the deletions are finished would mean landing a
check that fails on arrival, so it goes last on purpose.

One acceptance criterion needs restating before this is picked up. It asks
for a self-check demonstrating the chosen tool flags
`SqliteStorage::get_all_events`. That method no longer exists -- the events

pair that exists at the time, or assert the property directly (an item whose
only reference is a same-named inner function must still be reported).

Measured value so far, as an argument for eventually doing it: the four runs
drove "unreachable from main" from 222 items to well under half that, and
every cluster found was invisible to the occurrence-counting sweep that
produced the original beads.

title: The event-writer layer in storage::events is unreachable and drifting
description:
`src/storage/events.rs` reads as the storage layer's event-writing API. It is
not: the entire writer half is reachable only from that file's own test module.
Production writes events with inline SQL somewhere else, and the two have
diverged in a way that makes the dead API actively dangerous to reach for.

## What is dead

`insert_event` (`:61`) and all twelve typed wrappers built on it:

| Line | Function |
| --- | --- |
| `:97` | `insert_created_event` |
| `:106` | `insert_updated_event` |
| `:131` | `insert_status_changed_event` |
| `:154` | `insert_closed_event` |
| `:176` | `insert_reopened_event` |
| `:198` | `insert_commented_event` |
| `:220` | `insert_dependency_added_event` |
| `:244` | `insert_dependency_removed_event` |
| `:267` | `insert_label_added_event` |
| `:289` | `insert_label_removed_event` |
| `:311` | `insert_deleted_event` |
| `:333` | `insert_restored_event` |

plus `init_events_table` (`:518`), the `EVENTS_TABLE_SCHEMA` constant (`:19`)
that only it consumes, and `count_events` (`:481`). Every reference to every one
of them sits at a line number above `:523`, which is where
`#[cfg(test)] mod tests` begins.

Two read helpers are also dead as a pair rather than individually:
`SqliteStorage::get_all_events` (`src/storage/sqlite.rs:1955`) has no callers,
and it is the only caller of `events::get_all_events` (`:456`). A
reference-counting sweep will not spot this, because the wrapper and the inner
function share a name and each inflates the other's count — `rust-analyzer`'s
`findReferences` on the wrapper returns only its own definition.

`get_events` (`:361`) is the one writer-adjacent function that is genuinely
live: `sqlite.rs:10` imports it, and it is reached through
`SqliteStorage::get_events` and at `sqlite.rs:11202`.

## What production actually does

Events are written in one place — `src/storage/sqlite.rs:2845`, inside the
transaction-commit path:

```sql
INSERT INTO events (issue_id, event_type, actor, old_value, new_value,
                    comment, created_at, agent_name, harness, model)
VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)
```

Ten columns. `events::insert_event` writes seven, omitting `agent_name`,
`harness` and `model` entirely.

## Why that matters beyond the dead weight

**The dead API is a trap.** Those three columns are the issue #312 Tier 1
attribution capture. Anyone adding a new event type will find a file named
`events.rs` containing a well-documented `insert_status_changed_event` and use
it, and the resulting rows will silently carry no attribution. Nothing warns:
the columns are nullable by design (so events without attribution and older
databases stay valid), so the write succeeds and the audit trail is simply
thinner than it should be. The trap is not hypothetical — it is the obvious
thing to do.

**Two event types are unreachable.** `EventType::Updated` and
`EventType::DependencyRemoved` are constructed nowhere except inside
`insert_updated_event` (`:118`) and `insert_dependency_removed_event` (`:254`).
Both are dead, so no `br` command can write either type. They round-trip
correctly through `as_str`/`from_str` (`src/model/mod.rs:393`, `:401`, `:424`,
`:432`) and are covered by tests there, which is why nothing has noticed. Decide
deliberately whether the variants should be emitted (an `update` that changes a
field arguably *should* record an `updated` event, and `br dep remove` arguably
*should* record `dependency_removed`) or whether they are genuinely vestigial
and should go.

**The test coverage is illusory.** Roughly 400 lines of tests below `:523`
exercise this API. They pass, they are well written, and they assert nothing
about the code path that actually runs. That is worse than no tests, because
the file looks covered.

## Suggested shape of the fix

Deleting the writer layer wholesale is the simple option and is probably right,
but check the second bullet above first — if `Updated` / `DependencyRemoved`
should be emitted, that is a behaviour change to land separately, not something
to silently discard along with the dead code.

If instead the layer is kept and adopted, it has to grow the attribution
parameters and `sqlite.rs:2845` has to route through it; a half-migration where
some events carry attribution and some do not is the worst of the three
outcomes.

Either way `EVENTS_TABLE_SCHEMA` goes — see the sibling issue on the schema
drift, which is the reason it cannot simply be left lying around.

## Acceptance criteria

- No function in `src/storage/events.rs` is reachable only from that file's
  `#[cfg(test)]` module.
- `SqliteStorage::get_all_events` and `events::get_all_events` are either
  deleted or given a real caller.
- A deliberate, recorded decision on `EventType::Updated` and
  `EventType::DependencyRemoved`: either a command emits them and a test proves
  it, or the variants are removed along with their `as_str`/`from_str` arms.
- If any writer helper survives, it writes all ten columns including
  `agent_name` / `harness` / `model`, and a test asserts attribution survives a
  write through it.
- Test count is compared with `cargo nextest list --workspace` before and after
  and the diff of test *names* is explained — not reconciled by arithmetic.
- `env -u RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN task check` exits 0, and
  `cargo test --test licensing` passes after staging.
close_reason: Superseded by bds-1zd: the dead writer layer was deleted along with the whole events subsystem. Recording for the record that this ticket was wrong on one point -- EventType::Updated and EventType::DependencyRemoved were NOT unreachable; both were emitted in production from sqlite.rs (:3572, :9395 and :8550, :8610, :8661, :8769) via MutationContext. The sites this ticket inspected were the dead wrappers, not the live inline path. Investigation also established the layer was never wired: git log -S insert_event over the upstream storage layer returns no commits in its entire history, so nothing was lost in the port. 77507ff

title: Two events-table schemas disagree on the actor index
description:
The `events` table DDL exists twice, in `src/storage/schema.rs:169` and in
`EVENTS_TABLE_SCHEMA` at `src/storage/events.rs:19`. The column lists still
agree. The indexes no longer do, and one of the disagreements is a name
collision that SQLite resolves silently.

## The drift

| | `schema.rs:189-192` (production) | `events.rs:36-39` (tests only) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| issue index | `idx_events_issue ON events(issue_id)` | same |
| created index | `idx_events_created_at ON events(created_at)` | same |
| type index | `idx_events_type ON events(event_type)` | `idx_events_event_type ON events(event_type)` |
| actor index | `idx_events_actor ON events(actor) WHERE actor != ''` | `idx_events_actor ON events(actor)` |

The type index differs only in name, which is harmless in isolation — the two
would coexist as separate indexes.

The actor index is the problem: **same name, different definition.** One is a
partial index with a `WHERE actor != ''` predicate; the other indexes every
row, including the very common `actor = ''` case (the column is
`NOT NULL DEFAULT ''`). Both are written as `CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS`, so
whichever statement runs first creates the index and the other becomes a silent
no-op. No error, no warning, nothing in the schema-version machinery notices,
because from `IF NOT EXISTS`'s point of view an index by that name exists and
the job is done.

There is a third copy at `schema.rs:1800-1802` that agrees with the production
one; worth folding into the same fix so the count goes to one rather than two.

## Consequences

**Production is fine today, by accident.** `init_events_table` — the only
consumer of `EVENTS_TABLE_SCHEMA` — is dead outside of `events.rs`'s own test
module (see the sibling issue on the dead event-writer layer). So a real
database always gets `schema.rs`'s partial index. Nothing is currently
mis-indexed on disk.

**The tests in `events.rs` validate a schema production does not have.** They
build their in-memory database from `EVENTS_TABLE_SCHEMA`, so any query
behaviour they assert around actor filtering is being checked against a full
index while the shipped database has a partial one. For a predicate like
`WHERE actor = ''` those are not the same plan, and the partial index cannot
serve it at all. This is the concrete reason the duplication is worth
eliminating rather than merely tidying.

**It is a live footgun for whoever reunifies them.** If someone adopts
`EVENTS_TABLE_SCHEMA` as the single source (the natural instinct — it is the
one that lives next to the events code), production quietly switches to a
larger, full index on a column that is empty for most rows, and no test fails.

## Fix

Delete `EVENTS_TABLE_SCHEMA` and `init_events_table`, keep `schema.rs` as the
single definition, and point the `events.rs` tests at `schema::execute_batch`
with the real schema — they already import `crate::storage::schema::execute_batch`
at `:527`, so the wiring is mostly there. Fold `schema.rs:1800-1802` in too.

If for some reason a standalone events-only DDL constant must survive, it has
to be *derived from* the production schema rather than transcribed beside it,
and a test has to assert the two produce identical `sqlite_master` rows.

## Verification

After the change, on a freshly initialised workspace:

```sh
sqlite3 .beads/beads.db \
  "SELECT name, sql FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='index' AND tbl_name='events' ORDER BY name;"
```

should list exactly one actor index, with the `WHERE actor != ''` predicate
intact, and the same set should come back from whatever the `events.rs` tests
build.

## Acceptance criteria

- Exactly one `events` table DDL exists in the tree.
- The `events.rs` tests build their schema from that definition, not from a
  transcription of it.
- A test asserts the index set on the events table — by name *and* by `sql`
  text, so a future partial-vs-full divergence fails rather than no-ops.
- `env -u RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN task check` exits 0.
close_reason: Superseded by bds-1zd: both events-table DDLs are gone, along with EVENTS_TABLE_SCHEMA, init_events_table and the whole table. The index-name collision it describes can no longer occur. 77507ff

title: Delete the residue of the removed count, lint and query commands
description:
`Commands` in `src/cli/mod.rs` has 23 variants, every one of them dispatched in
`src/main.rs`. There is no `count`, no `lint`, and no `query`. Support code for
all three is still in the tree — CLI argument structs, a completer, and eight
storage methods — and one piece of it costs real time on every config
tab-completion.

The history was squashed at 1.0.0, so `git log` does not show when the commands
went. It does not matter much: the code is unreachable now.

## `br query`

Three `clap` argument structs that no `Commands` variant holds:

- `QuerySaveArgs` — `src/cli/mod.rs:2165`
- `QueryRunArgs` — `:2180`
- `QueryDeleteArgs` — `:2192`

`rust-analyzer` `findReferences` on `QuerySaveArgs` returns its own definition
and nothing else.

Behind them sits a whole completion chain that exists only to serve them:

- `saved_query_completer` (`:591`) — attached only to `QueryRunArgs.name` and
  `QueryDeleteArgs.name`
- `CompletionConfigIndex.saved_queries` (`:85`) — read only by that completer
- `saved_queries_from_db` (`:221`) and `SAVED_QUERY_PREFIX` (`:197`) — the only
  producers of that field

`saved_queries_from_db` is not free, and it runs on a code path that is still
reachable. That is written up separately as its own bug, because it is a
performance defect rather than a tidiness one; it is fixed by this deletion.

## `br count`

- `CountBy` (`src/cli/mod.rs:1694`) — a `ValueEnum` with `Status`, `Priority`,
  `Type`, `Assignee`, `Label` variants, held by no argument struct
- `SqliteStorage::count_default_visible_statuses` (`src/storage/sqlite.rs:5288`)
- `…_types` (`:5297`), `…_assignees` (`:5306`), `…_priorities` (`:5318`),
  `…_labels` (`:5346`)
- `SqliteStorage::count_labels_with_filters` (`:5443`)

The last one names the removed command in its own doc comment: *"mirrors the
label grouping semantics used by `br count --by label`: each labeled issue
contributes once per label, and unlabeled issues contribute to the synthetic
`(no labels)` bucket."* That is a precise description of behaviour nothing can
invoke.

## `br lint`

- `SqliteStorage::list_lint_issues_for_command_output`
  (`src/storage/sqlite.rs:4843`), whose doc reads *"List lint command issues
  without hydrating fields lint never inspects… falls back to `list_issues` if
  the filter shape expands beyond what `br lint` currently uses."*

## Before deleting

These are not obviously abandoned — they are careful, documented, working code
for features that once existed. Worth one deliberate decision rather than a
reflexive `rm`:

- Are `count` / `lint` / `query` coming back? If yes, the honest move is a bead
  describing the intent, and a `#[allow(dead_code)]` with a comment pointing at
  it, so the next sweep does not re-litigate this. Leaving unexplained dead code
  as a bet on the future is what produced the current state.
- `count_labels_with_filters` in particular encodes a non-obvious semantic
  choice (issues counted once per label, plus a synthetic no-label bucket). If
  `br stats` or any future grouping wants that, the logic is worth keeping even
  though the entry point went. Check `src/cli/commands/stats.rs` before
  discarding it.
- The `saved_query:` config-key prefix may exist in real users' databases. If
  so, deleting the reader leaves orphan rows that nothing will ever clean up or
  surface. That is probably acceptable — config rows are cheap — but it should
  be a decision, and if `br query` is not coming back it is worth saying so in
  `docs/CLI_REFERENCE.md` for anyone who has such rows.

## Acceptance criteria

- `br query`, `br count` and `br lint` leave no unreferenced code behind: no
  argument structs, no completer, no storage method that exists only for them.
- Anything deliberately retained for a planned return carries an explicit
  `#[allow(dead_code)]` and a comment naming the bead that will consume it.
- `br config get <TAB>` no longer touches the database (see the sibling
  performance bug for how to verify).
- Shell completion still works end to end for `br config get`, `br config set`
  and the issue-ID completers — the completion index is shared machinery and
  this touches part of it.
- `env -u RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN task check` exits 0, and `cargo test --test licensing`
  passes after staging.
close_reason:
Done in 0510585.

Deleted, per the bead's inventory:

- query: QuerySaveArgs, QueryRunArgs, QueryDeleteArgs, saved_query_completer,
  CompletionConfigIndex.saved_queries, saved_queries_from_db,
  SAVED_QUERY_PREFIX, and the unit test that covered the reader.
- count: CountBy, count_default_visible_{statuses,types,assignees,priorities,
  labels}, count_default_visible_text_groups, count_labels_with_filters.
- lint: list_lint_issues_for_command_output and lint_command_issue_from_row,
  its only row mapper.

Roughly 550 lines, 428 of them in storage/sqlite.rs.

The bead asked for three deliberate decisions rather than a reflexive rm:

1. Not coming back. Nothing is retained and no #[allow(dead_code)] was added.
2. count_labels_with_filters: checked stats.rs as instructed. `br stats
   --by-label` computes its own breakdown from list_label_pairs_unordered,
   including the same synthetic no-label bucket, so the semantics were never
   only here.
3. Orphan `saved_query:` config rows: nothing in docs/ or README.md ever
   mentioned `br query`, `br count` or `br lint`, so there is no doc
   section to amend. Rows in an existing database are left in place, unread.

The count cluster turned out to be entirely self-referential -- every caller
of the private helpers was itself one of the dead public methods -- which is
why it could go whole. count_default_visible_single_label and
count_default_visible_issues stay: they have a live caller in
count_issues_with_filters.

Verification: task check exits 0; suite 3151 passed, 4 skipped. Test count
reconciled by name diff, not arithmetic: 1 removed
(cli::tests::test_saved_queries_from_db_...), 2 added (the bds-xtg regression
module).

title: Config-key completion copies the whole database to feed a dead completer
description:
Pressing TAB after `br config get` copies the entire SQLite database family —
`.db`, `-wal` and `-shm` — into a temporary directory, opens the copy, and scans
its `config` table. The result of that scan feeds exactly one consumer: a
completer attached to two argument structs that no `Commands` variant holds, so
nothing can ever display it.

## The chain

`src/cli/mod.rs`:

```
config_key_completer            (:598)   <- wired at :2054, :2073
config_key_assignment_completer (:605)   <- wired at :2064
  -> config_index()             (:203)   OnceLock::get_or_init
     -> build_config_index()    (:317)
        -> saved_queries_from_db(:221)
           -> config::with_database_family_snapshot
```

and `src/config/mod.rs:2257`:

```rust
pub(crate) fn with_database_family_snapshot<T, F>(db_path: &Path, read: F) -> Result<T> {
    let snapshot_dir = tempdir()...;
    let snapshot_db_path = copy_database_family_to_directory(db_path, snapshot_dir.path())?;
    read(&snapshot_db_path)
}
```

`build_config_index` needs the DB for nothing else — `config_keys` is assembled
entirely from `default_config_layer()`, `load_legacy_user_config()`,
`load_user_config()`, `ConfigLayer::from_env()` and `load_project_config()`,
all of which read YAML or the environment. The single `saved_queries.extend(...)`
line at `:334` is what drags the database in.

And `saved_queries` is read only by `saved_query_completer` (`:591`), which is
attached only to `QueryRunArgs.name` (`:2182`) and `QueryDeleteArgs.name`
(`:2194`) — argument structs for a `br query` command that no longer exists.

## Cost

The snapshot is a full byte copy, not a link or a page-level snapshot. On this
repository's own workspace `.beads/beads.db` is 1.3 MB before counting the WAL,
and that copy happens synchronously in the completion subprocess, i.e. in the
interactive path between the user pressing TAB and seeing candidates. On a
large workspace it scales with database size, and it happens on a keystroke.

Two mitigating facts, so the severity is not overstated: `config_index()` is a
`OnceLock`, so it happens at most once per completion subprocess; and the whole
path is gated behind `CompleteEnv::with_factory(Cli::command).complete()` in
`main.rs`, so ordinary `br` invocations never reach it. This is a
tab-completion latency bug, not a general one.

The snapshot itself is not gratuitous where it *is* needed — copying the family
is how a reader avoids `PRAGMA busy_timeout` contention against a live writer,
and `saved_queries_from_db` even sets `busy_timeout=0` on the copy. The defect
is that this particular caller needs no database at all.

## Fix

Deleting the `br query` residue removes this by construction — that is the
sibling issue, and it is the right fix. This bead exists separately because the
cost is a user-visible symptom worth verifying independently of the cleanup, and
because if the residue is retained for a planned `br query` revival, the
snapshot on the completion path still has to go: it can be made lazy (only
resolve saved queries when `saved_query_completer` is actually invoked) rather
than eager inside `build_config_index`.

## Verification

Before the fix, with a workspace present:

```sh
# watch for the temp-dir copy on a config completion
COMPLETE=zsh br config get '' >/dev/null
```

Instrument `with_database_family_snapshot` with a `tracing::debug!`, or strace /
`fs_usage` the completion subprocess, and observe the `.db` / `-wal` reads. After
the fix, a config-key completion should touch no file under `.beads/` except the
YAML config layers.

## Acceptance criteria

- A config-key completion performs no database open and no database copy.
- Config-key completion still returns the full key set from all five layers
  (default, legacy user, user, project, env).
- A test covers the "completion does not open the database" property, so the
  dependency cannot creep back in — asserting on candidates alone would not
  catch a reintroduced snapshot.
- `env -u RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN task check` exits 0.
close_reason:
Fixed in 0510585.

Reproduced empirically before fixing, which the bead asked for. A probe in
`with_database_family_snapshot` on a build of the pre-fix tree:

    COMPLETE=bash _CLAP_COMPLETE_INDEX=3 br -- br config get ""
    XTG-PROBE: database family snapshot of .../.beads/beads.db

After the fix the same invocation prints no probe line, and the candidate
list is byte-identical to the released 1.1.1 binary's. `br config set` and
the issue-ID completer (`br show`) are byte-identical too. (The bead's
suggested `COMPLETE=zsh br config get ''` does not drive clap's dynamic
completion; the protocol needs the `-- br ...` separator and
_CLAP_COMPLETE_INDEX, as above.)

The fix is the sibling deletion (bds-y6o), as the bead predicted: nothing
survives that wants saved queries, so `build_config_index` no longer
resolves `paths.db_path` at all. The whole completion path is now
database-free -- the issue-ID completers read issues.jsonl line by line.

Worth recording, because it changes what a regression test can be: the old
path swallowed every error, so a completion that copied the database and one
that did not produced identical bytes. There is no behavioural signal. The
guard in tests/repro/config_completion_no_db.rs is therefore source-level --
src/cli/mod.rs holds every completer and must contain no
`with_database_family_snapshot`, `Connection::open` or
`SqliteStorage::open`. Verified non-vacuous by appending one of those
strings to the file and watching the test fail with the intended message.

title: An unknown issue ID never gets a "did you mean" suggestion
description:
`br` ships a Levenshtein-style ID suggester, `find_similar_ids`
(`src/error/structured.rs:1029`), and a structured-error constructor that turns
its output into a *"Did you mean 'bds-abc12'?"* hint. Neither is reachable. A
mistyped issue ID gets a flat `Issue not found: bds-abcl2` with the generic
hint `Run 'br list' to see available issues.`, and a `--json` consumer gets a
context object containing nothing but the string it already passed in.

## Evidence

`find_similar_ids` has exactly three references (`rust-analyzer`
`findReferences`):

- `:1029` — its own definition
- `:1153` — its own unit test, `test_find_similar_ids`
- `:348` — inside `StructuredError::issue_not_found`

and `StructuredError::issue_not_found` (`:347`) has exactly one reference: its
own definition. Nothing constructs it.

The live path is `StructuredError::from_error`, called from `main.rs` for every
error the CLI renders. Its arm for this case is `src/error/structured.rs:567`:

```rust
BeadsError::IssueNotFound { id } => {
    (ErrorCode::IssueNotFound, Some(json!({"searched_id": id})))
}
```

and the matching hint, `generate_hint` at `:736`:

```rust
BeadsError::IssueNotFound { .. } => {
    Some("Run 'br list' to see available issues.".to_string())
}
```

Compare what the dead constructor would have produced (`:347-370`): a
`similar_ids` array in the context, and one of three hints — *"Did you mean
'X'?"* for a single candidate, *"Did you mean one of: X, Y, Z?"* for several,
and the `br list` line only as the fallback when there is genuinely nothing
close.

## Why this is a gap and not just dead code

The information needed is already in hand at the exact moment the error is
built. `IdResolver::resolve_fallible` (`src/util/id.rs:790`) runs three steps —
exact match, prefix normalisation, substring match on the hash portion — and
reaches `:858`:

```rust
Err(BeadsError::IssueNotFound { id: input.to_string() })
```

only after `substring_match_fn` has returned an empty vector. The candidate
universe is one call away and the resolver is already holding the closure that
enumerates it (`SqliteStorage` provides it via `find_matching_ids` at
`sqlite.rs:8068`).

The suggester is also better than the resolver's own substring step, not
redundant with it: substring matching cannot help with a *transposition* or a
*wrong character*, which is what a typo usually is. `bds-abcl2` for `bds-abc12`
matches nothing by substring and would be caught by edit distance.

This matters more than average here because IDs are short opaque hashes that
agents and humans both copy by hand, and because `br`'s whole posture is
agent-first: the `--json` error object is a documented integration surface, and
`similar_ids` in it is directly actionable by a caller that wants to retry.

## Two ways to close it

1. **Enrich the `from_error` arm.** Requires plumbing the candidate list into
   `BeadsError::IssueNotFound`, e.g. a `similar: Vec<String>` field populated by
   the resolver. Most direct, but touches an error variant constructed in many
   places, all of which would need to decide what to pass.
2. **Have the resolver build the richer error.** `resolve_fallible` already has
   both the input and the lookup closures; it could ask for near-misses on the
   failure path and construct the suggestion there. Narrower blast radius, and
   it puts the logic where the knowledge is.

Option 2 is likely the smaller change. Either way `StructuredError::issue_not_found`
is the code to route through rather than reimplement — it is already written and
already has the singular/plural/fallback hint shaping.

Two sibling constructors are dead in the same way and should be settled in the
same pass, since the question is identical: `StructuredError::cycle_detected`
(`:401`) and `StructuredError::invalid_type` (`:483`). Check whether the
corresponding `from_error` arms lose anything by comparison — `invalid_type`'s
does run `detect_type_intent` (`:749`), so that one may already be adequate and
the constructor simply redundant.

## Acceptance criteria

- `br show <mistyped-id>` on a workspace containing a near-miss suggests it, in
  both text and `--json` output.
- The `--json` error object for `ISSUE_NOT_FOUND` carries a `similar_ids` array
  (empty when there is no near match), and `docs/CLI_REFERENCE.md`'s JSON error
  schema documents it.
- With no near match, the existing `Run 'br list'` hint is what appears — the
  fallback is preserved, not replaced.
- `find_similar_ids` has a caller on the production path, verified by
  `findReferences` rather than by a passing test.
- `StructuredError::cycle_detected` and `StructuredError::invalid_type` are
  either wired up or deleted, with the reason recorded.
- `env -u RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN task check` exits 0.
close_reason:
Fixed in 4c629ec.

Wired at the render boundary, which is a third option the bead did not list
and which avoids the tradeoff it identified between its two. `handle_error`
in main.rs is the single point all 11 CLI error paths funnel through, so the
suggestion is attached once there rather than by widening
`BeadsError::IssueNotFound` -- constructed at 31 production sites, most of
them storage functions holding one ID and no catalogue. Option 2 as written
could not work either: `resolve_fallible` returns a `BeadsError`, so anything
it computed would still need somewhere in the variant to ride.

Candidates come from issues.jsonl rather than the database: no lock on a path
that may be failing *because* the database is busy, and it is the same source
the shell completers read, so a suggestion cannot name an ID that TAB would
not have offered. The cost is that an issue created since the last export is
not a candidate.

## The part that was not just wiring

The suggester could not have been switched on as it stood, and this is the
main finding. `find_similar_ids` filtered on a hardcoded `distance <= 3`.
Beads IDs are a shared prefix plus a short random suffix, so two unrelated
IDs differ by exactly the suffix length -- with a 3-character suffix every ID
in a workspace sits at distance 3 from every other. Measured on the 9 open
beads at the time: a one-character typo of bds-k7e put all 9 within the
threshold. The feature would have shipped as "Did you mean one of:" followed
by three alphabetically-first strangers.

Now a single edit, with Damerau rather than plain Levenshtein so a transposed
pair costs 1 rather than 2 -- the bead named transpositions specifically, and
at a bound of 1 plain Levenshtein would have excluded every one of them.

A length-scaled bound was tried first and is also wrong, which is worth
recording because it looks reasonable: the prefix is shared by every ID in a
workspace, so it contributes length without contributing anything that
distinguishes one ID from another. A workspace with a long prefix would relax
the bound to 2 while still having only 3 characters that differ. The
end-to-end tests caught it in a temp directory whose name became the prefix.

## Acceptance criteria

- Text and --json both suggest the near miss. Verified end to end.
- `context.similar_ids` present, `[]` when nothing is close. Documented.
- The `Run 'br list'` fallback is preserved, with its own test.
- `find_similar_ids` has a production caller: handle_error ->
  with_id_suggestions -> issue_not_found -> find_similar_ids. Verified by
  reference search, not by a passing test.
- Sibling constructors settled: see below.
- task check exits 0. 3138 tests, 4 removed / 14 added by name diff.

## Sibling constructors

`ambiguous_id`, `cycle_detected`, `not_initialized`, `invalid_priority`,
`invalid_status` and `invalid_type` were dead the same way, and all six are
deleted as redundant -- the live `from_error` arms produce the same code,
hint and context. Their four unit tests are rewritten against `from_error`,
so they now assert what a user sees instead of what an uncalled constructor
would have returned.

One difference is not redundant and is filed as bds-b0m: `generate_hint`
returns `BeadsError::suggestion()` before reaching its own intent-detection
arms, and `suggestion()` is `Some` for exactly the priority/status/type
variants those arms handle. So `detect_priority_intent` resolves "high" to 1
and the answer is discarded -- the user gets the static range text. The good
hint does reach the --json context, just not the hint field.

## Also fixed

docs/CLI_REFERENCE.md's Error Object documented `error_code`, `kind` and
`recovery_hints`. None of the three exists; the real envelope is
`{error: {code, message, hint, retryable, context}}`. Rewritten against
actual output, since `similar_ids` could not be documented into a schema that
was fiction.
