description: An epic with open children cannot be closed and its children cannot be moved out, because parentage is recorded both in the parent-child dep row and in the issue ID, and the two are free to disagree. Make the ID authoritative so disagreement is unrepresentable: a dotted prefix always names the real parent, and having a parent always implies a dotted ID. Architecture: one transactional rename_issue storage primitive with subtree cascade and deferred FK checks; a tombstone at the old ID plus a former_ids array on the issue for redirects; renumber-on-attach and refuse-on-detach at every chokepoint that can set or clear a parent-child edge; and a divergence detector in br info --projections for violations arriving via JSONL import, which cannot be enforced. Tech stack: Rust, SQLite via rusqlite, cargo-nextest.
design:
# Make the hierarchical ID authoritative, and add `br detach`

## The problem

An epic with open children cannot be closed, and there is no way to move a
child out from under it. `--force` is the only escape, which defeats the guard
rather than satisfying it.

The cause is that parentage is recorded in two independent places that are free
to disagree:

1. the `parent-child` row in `dependencies`, and
2. the issue ID itself (`ab-xxx.1`).

`br update <child> --parent ""` clears (1) — `resolve_parent_update` in
`src/cli/commands/update.rs:1399` maps `""` to `ParentUpdatePlan::Clear`, and it
works. But `close` consults (2) through a second, independent guard:
`get_open_dot_notation_children` (`src/storage/sqlite.rs:7138`) is a bare
`SELECT id FROM issues WHERE id LIKE 'ab-xxx.%'` that never reads the
dependencies table. So the parent link disappears and the epic still refuses to
close:

```
$ br update ab-ygq.1 --parent ""      -> Updated ab-ygq.1
$ br dep list ab-ygq.1                -> No dependencies for ab-ygq.1
$ br close ab-ygq                     -> epic has 1 open dot-notation child: ab-ygq.1
```

The same divergence is a plain defect for reparenting. Moving a child to a
different epic leaves the *original* epic permanently unclosable, despite having
no children by any dependency measure:

```
$ br update ab-l04.1 --parent ab-fb6   -> child now depends on ab-fb6
$ br close ab-l04                      -> epic has 1 open dot-notation child: ab-l04.1
```

That guard is not itself wrong. It was added to catch legacy and imported
children whose dep row is missing, and it still has that job. What is wrong is
that the mutation paths let the ID go stale underneath it.

## The decision

**The ID is authoritative.** Rather than teaching the guard to tolerate
disagreement, make disagreement unrepresentable:

> A dotted prefix always names the real parent, and having a parent always
> implies a dotted ID.

Every operation that changes parentage therefore also changes the ID. Detaching
a child means giving it a new flat ID; attaching one means renumbering it under
its new parent. `get_open_dot_notation_children` then needs no change at all,
and keeps its original legacy-data role.

## Architecture

### One storage primitive

```rust
fn rename_issue(&mut self, old_id: &str, new_id: &str, actor: &str) -> Result<()>
```

Everything else is a caller. Four details govern its correctness:

- **Descendants move with it.** Renaming `ab-xxx.1` to `ab-yyy.3` must rename
  `ab-xxx.1.1` to `ab-yyy.3.1`, at every depth and in every status. The existing
  scan is open-only and one level deep, so this needs a generalized sibling
  query rather than a reuse.
- **Foreign keys do not cascade.** `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON`
  (`src/storage/schema.rs:507`) with no `ON UPDATE` clause anywhere means
  `UPDATE issues SET id = ?` fails outright while child rows exist. Use
  `PRAGMA defer_foreign_keys = ON`, which is transaction-scoped and resets
  itself, in preference to the global `foreign_keys = OFF` toggle at
  `schema.rs:930`.
- **`dependencies.depends_on_id` has no foreign key.** It was removed
  deliberately to allow external issue references (`schema.rs:132`), so inbound
  edges pointing at the renamed issue are unconstrained text and nothing will
  complain if the rewrite misses them. This is the likeliest bug in the feature.
- **Child counters only ever increase.** Bump the new parent's counter; never
  decrement the old parent's. Reusing `ab-xxx.1` would silently redirect every
  stale reference to the original occupant onto a different issue.

The rewrite covers `issues` plus every table holding an issue ID:
`dependencies` (both columns), `labels`, `comments`, `dirty_issues`,
`export_hashes`, `blocked_issues_cache`, `child_counters`, `close_metadata`, and
any others present in the schema at implementation time.

**A hand-maintained list of those tables would rot.** Instead, a test walks
`PRAGMA table_info` across every table, identifies columns holding issue IDs,
and fails when one appears that `rename_issue` does not cover — the same
approach `tests/licensing.rs` takes to enumerating tracked files.

### The old ID: tombstone plus `former_ids`

Two complementary records, because they survive different things.

- **A tombstone at the old ID.** `br delete` already writes `status='tombstone'`
  rows that round-trip through JSONL and are collected by `br delete --hard`.
  Reusing that gives an O(1) redirect at resolver step 1, and propagates the
  disappearance through JSONL so another clone's copy of `ab-xxx.1` merges as a
  tombstone instead of resurrecting as a second issue. Tombstones are already
  excluded from `br list` and from the open-children scan, so nothing else
  needs to learn about them.
- **`former_ids: Vec<String>` on `Issue`**, with
  `#[serde(default, skip_serializing_if = "Vec::is_empty")]`. Permanent
  provenance that outlives tombstone collection, and it carries the forward
  direction so `br show ab-k9p` can report what it used to be called.

**Every renamed node gets both, at any depth.** A rename that cascades through a
subtree gives each descendant its own tombstone and its own `former_ids` entry,
exactly as the top-level node gets. This was decided against the alternative of
recording only the top-level node, which was tried first: it left old descendant
IDs unresolvable (`find_id_by_former_id` is an exact match with no prefix
splicing, so there is nothing for it to find), and — the deciding reason — it
left a deep rename only half-propagated. The tombstone exists so another clone
merges a disappearance rather than re-creating a live issue; skipping it for
descendants reproduces exactly that failure one level down. The JSONL cost is
proportional to the subtree actually renamed, which is bounded and rare.

### Resolver

`IdResolver::resolve_fallible` (`src/util/id.rs:589`) currently tries exact
match, prefix-completed exact match, then substring match — and that last step
already calls `find_ids_by_hash`, which is `SELECT id FROM issues` pulled
entirely into memory (`sqlite.rs:7052`).

The `former_ids` lookup slots in ahead of that substring scan. It only runs when
both exact-match steps have already missed, so the hot path — a fully spelled
current ID — never touches it, and the path it does join already costs a full
scan. A derived `former_id_index` table for O(1) lookup is deliberately deferred:
the array on the issue stays authoritative, so it can be added later with no
change to the data model or the JSONL format, following the existing
`blocked_issues_cache` / `export_hashes` / `child_counters` pattern.

## Enforcement points

Every path that can set or clear a `parent-child` edge, because a missed one
reintroduces the divergence:

| Entry point | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| `br create --parent X` | already mints `X.n` — correct today, no change |
| `br create --dep parent-child:X` | refuse, point at `--parent` (`create.rs:709`) |
| `br update <id> --parent X` | renumber to `X.n` |
| `br update <id> --parent ""` | refuse, point at `br detach` |
| `br dep add <id> X --type parent-child` | renumber to `X.n` |
| `br dep remove <id> X`, edge is parent-child | refuse, point at `br detach` (`dep.rs:693`) |
| `br dep import` | same rule per row, in the bulk path |
| JSONL import | cannot be enforced — see below |

The two operations that *break* a parent link both refuse and route through
`br detach`, so exactly one command renames on detach and one renames on attach.
Refusing `--parent ""` rather than silently performing the detach is deliberate:
a rename is consequential and visible, and should not be a side effect of an
update flag.

### `br detach <id>...`

| ID shape | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| dotted | mint a flat ID via the same `IdGenerator` path `br create` uses with no parent, rewrite, drop the `parent-child` dep |
| flat | drop the dep only; no rename is needed |

### The door that cannot be locked

JSONL import accepts arbitrary data, including legacy repositories that already
violate the invariant. It therefore cannot enforce it, which is why the
invariant needs a detector as well as enforcement. `--force` on `close` remains
available for the same reason.

The detector belongs in `br info --projections`
(`build_projection_info`, `src/cli/commands/info.rs:277`), which already reports
graph-integrity parity — cache-versus-direct row counts, mismatched rows, child
counter rows — and is documented as "diagnostic metadata about the workspace".
It is **not** `src/health.rs`: despite the name, that module classifies
*workspace file* anomalies (missing database, truncated WAL, conflict markers in
the JSONL) and is surfaced through `br sync --status`. Its own doc comment
explicitly declines to classify data-level drift, on the grounds that the
database is a derived cache of the JSONL and the remedy for disagreement is to
rebuild it. Hierarchy divergence is the opposite kind of problem — it lives in
the JSONL itself and a rebuild preserves it faithfully. There is no `br health`
command.

## Features

1. **`rename_issue` storage primitive** — transactional multi-table rewrite,
   subtree cascade, deferred FK checks, plus the `PRAGMA table_info`
   introspection test that fails when a new ID-bearing column appears.
2. **`former_ids` and the tombstone redirect** — model field, schema column,
   JSONL round-trip, tombstone written at the old ID, resolver fallback ahead of
   the substring scan.
3. **`br detach`** — the command, both ID shapes, batch IDs, JSON output.
4. **Renumber-on-attach and the refusals** — all six chokepoints in the table
   above, each with the error text pointing at `br detach`.
5. **`br info --projections` divergence check** — detect and report imported
   violations alongside the existing projection parity counts.

## Acceptance criteria

- An epic whose children have all been detached closes without `--force`.
- Reparenting a child to another epic renumbers it, and the original epic then
  closes without `--force`.
- `br update <dotted-id> --parent ""` and `br dep remove` on a `parent-child`
  edge both fail with an error naming `br detach`.
- After a rename, no row in any table still references the old ID, verified by
  the introspection test rather than an enumerated list.
- `br show <old-id>` resolves to the renamed issue; `br show <new-id> --json`
  reports the old ID in `former_ids`.
- Renaming a child with grandchildren moves the whole subtree, in every status.
- A detached ID is never reissued to a later child of the original parent.
- `former_ids` and the tombstone survive a JSONL export/import round-trip.
- `br info --projections` reports an imported issue whose dotted prefix
  disagrees with its `parent-child` dep.
- The reparent defect has a regression module under `tests/repro/`.

## Global Constraints

Every task's requirements implicitly include this section. Values are copied
verbatim from `CLAUDE.md` and the spec.

**Toolchain**

- Prefix every `cargo` / `rustc` / `task` invocation with `env -u RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN`.
  There is no `rust-toolchain.toml`; a stale exported `RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN` silently
  builds on nightly and still reports success.
- The gate is `env -u RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN task check`: `toolchain:check`,
  `format:check`, `lint` (clippy over every target, pedantic + nursery), then
  `test`. It is what CI runs and it must pass before this work merges.
- **Do not run the full gate per task.** It costs two-plus minutes and would
  dominate this plan's wall clock. Per task, run `cargo fmt` and the scoped
  `cargo nextest run -E '<filter>'` that the task brief names. The controller
  runs `task check` at feature boundaries and before the final review. If a task
  genuinely needs the full gate — schema changes, a shared trait, anything with
  blast radius past its own files — say so in the report and let the controller
  decide rather than running it yourself.
- `task test` needs **cargo-nextest** on `PATH`, and runs the doctests as a
  separate second command. Do not replace it with a bare `cargo nextest run`.
- `rust-version = "1.97.1"` in `Cargo.toml` is the support floor; `1.95` is the
  measured minimum. `tests/toolchain_floor.rs` fails if the manifest key, the
  bisection comment above it, and the CLAUDE.md paragraph drift apart. No task
  here should need to touch any of them.

**Commits**

- Commit messages must parse as **Conventional Commits** — `.cliff.toml` builds
  `CHANGELOG.md` from them and a commit that does not parse is missing from the
  release notes. Accepted: `feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `chore`, `build`, `ci`, `test`,
  `perf`, `style`, `refactor`, `revert`, plus a `!` breaking marker.
  **`spec:` and `plan:` are rejected.**
- **Never add AI or agent attribution trailers** — no `Co-Authored-By` naming an
  assistant, no `Generated with …`, no variant, in any commit, PR body, tag or
  release note. This overrides any harness default; strip one if a tool adds it.
- Stage `.beads/` with the work so bead state rides the task's own commit.
- Do not skip hooks and do not add `--no-verify`.

**Licensing guard**

- `tests/licensing.rs` sweeps every git-tracked file for substrings naming an
  upstream project or someone else's filesystem path. Lineage lives in
  `NOTICE.md` only — link to it rather than restating it.
- After staging any new or edited tracked file, run
  `env -u RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN cargo test --test licensing`.
- Never describe this project as plain MIT-licensed. `Cargo.toml` uses
  `license-file` because the licence carries a rider with no SPDX identifier.

**Test placement**

- Tests are grouped into a handful of binaries. Add a file to `tests/<group>/`
  **and** a `#[path]` line to the matching crate root — do not add a new
  top-level `tests/*.rs`.
  - `tests/e2e.rs` + `tests/e2e/*.rs` — drive `br` as a subprocess
  - `tests/storage.rs` + `tests/storage/*.rs` — SQLite, JSONL mirror, sync
  - `tests/repro.rs` + `tests/repro/*.rs` — one module per bug that happened
- `extern crate test_support as common;` is legal only at a crate root; inside a
  module write `use crate::common;`.
- insta snapshots live beside the asserting file and are named after the module
  path, so moving a test moves and renames its `.snap`.
- Verify any change in the test total by diffing
  `env -u RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN cargo nextest list --workspace` before and after.
  **Never** reconcile it by arithmetic.
- If you add a caller of `test_support::workspace_replay_test_guard()`, add it to
  the filter in `.config/nextest.toml` — nextest runs each test in its own
  process, so a `static Mutex` does not serialise across them.

**Schema**

- `CURRENT_SCHEMA_VERSION` is **17** (`src/storage/schema.rs:10`). The
  `former_ids` column migration takes it to **18**.
- Migrations are idempotent and guarded: `user_version < N && table_exists(…) &&
  !column_exists(…)`, and skipped when the table was just rebuilt from scratch
  (`!issues_rebuilt`). Follow the v10 `source_repo_path` / v11 `agent_context`
  pattern at `schema.rs:1570-1597`.
- All writes go through `SqliteStorage::with_write_transaction`
  (`src/storage/sqlite.rs:1436`), which owns `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`, retry and
  rollback. Do not hand-roll `BEGIN`/`COMMIT` in new code.

**The invariant this project establishes**

- A dotted prefix always names the real parent, and having a parent always
  implies a dotted ID.
- Foreign keys are enforced (`PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON`, `schema.rs:507`) and no
  FK declares `ON UPDATE`, so `UPDATE issues SET id = ?` fails while child rows
  exist. **Use `SqliteStorage::mutate`** (`sqlite.rs:2604`), the repo's universal
  write helper: it suppresses foreign keys for the closure and restores them on
  both the `Ok` and `Err` paths, escalating a restore failure into an error
  (`finish_foreign_key_suppressed_result`, `sqlite.rs:972`).

  *Ruling, bds-a23.1.2 review.* This constraint originally mandated
  transaction-scoped `PRAGMA defer_foreign_keys = ON` instead. The two differ in
  kind: `defer_foreign_keys` postpones checks to COMMIT, so a stranded reference
  still faults loudly, whereas `mutate`'s `foreign_keys = OFF` disables checking
  entirely and a table missing from `ID_BEARING_COLUMNS` dangles silently. The
  repo owner ruled for codebase consistency: `mutate` is what every other write
  uses, and hand-rolling a one-off transaction shape here costs more than the
  loud failure buys. The backstop is bds-a23.1.3's `PRAGMA table_info`
  introspection guard — which, note, cannot catch IDs buried inside JSON blob
  columns such as `blocked_issues_cache.blocked_by`.
- `dependencies.depends_on_id` has **no** foreign key — removed deliberately to
  allow external issue references (`schema.rs:132`). Nothing will fault if a
  rewrite misses it.
- Child counters only ever increase. Never decrement the old parent's counter; a
  reissued ID silently redirects stale references to a different issue.

**Remote**

- Never `git push`, open/merge/comment on a PR, cut a release, or make any
  non-GET `gh api` call without asking and receiving a yes. Reading (`gh pr
  list`, `gh run view`, `gh api` GETs) needs no approval. Local work —
  committing, branching, resetting — is outside this rule.

title: Introspection guard for ID-bearing columns

design:
### Task 3: The introspection guard — fail when a new ID-bearing column appears

`ID_BEARING_COLUMNS` is a hand-written list, and hand-written lists of schema
facts rot. Someone adds a table six months from now, `rename_issue` silently
stops covering it, and the only symptom is a dangling reference nobody notices
until an unrelated query returns wrong rows.

This test makes that impossible: it reads the live schema, works out which
columns hold issue IDs, and fails when one is missing from the list. It is the
same move `tests/licensing.rs` makes by enumerating every git-tracked file
rather than trusting a maintained list of files to check.

**Files:**
- Create: `tests/storage/rename_coverage.rs`
- Modify: `tests/storage.rs` (add the `#[path]` line)
- Modify: `src/storage/sqlite.rs` if the test finds a genuine gap

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: `beads::storage::ID_BEARING_COLUMNS` (Task 2). It is
  `pub(crate)` there — this test needs it visible, so promote it to `pub` and
  re-export it from `src/storage/mod.rs`. It is a schema fact, not an
  implementation detail, and the whole point is that it is checkable.
- Produces: nothing consumed by later tasks.

**How the test decides a column holds an issue ID.** Not by name matching, which
would miss `child_counters.parent_id` and falsely flag `comments.author`.
By declared foreign key plus an explicit exception list:

1. `PRAGMA foreign_key_list(<table>)` — any column with an FK referencing
   `issues` holds an issue ID. This catches all but one.
2. `dependencies.depends_on_id` has no FK by design, so it is a known addition.
3. Anything else is neither, and the test says so.

- [ ] **Step 3: Write the test**

Create `tests/storage/rename_coverage.rs`:

```rust
//! Guards `rename_issue`'s table list against schema drift.
//!
//! `ID_BEARING_COLUMNS` is hand-written, and a hand-written list of schema facts
//! rots the moment someone adds a table. This reads the live schema instead and
//! fails when the two disagree, so the gap is a red test rather than a dangling
//! reference discovered months later.

use crate::common;

use beads::storage::ID_BEARING_COLUMNS;
use common::test_db;
use std::collections::BTreeSet;

/// `dependencies.depends_on_id` holds an issue ID but declares no foreign key —
/// removed deliberately at `schema.rs:132` so `external:` references can dangle.
/// It is the one column the FK sweep cannot find on its own.
const FK_EXEMPT_ID_COLUMNS: &[(&str, &str)] = &[("dependencies", "depends_on_id")];

#[test]
fn every_id_bearing_column_is_covered_by_rename_issue() {
    let storage = test_db();
    let conn = storage.connection();

    let mut from_schema: BTreeSet<(String, String)> = FK_EXEMPT_ID_COLUMNS
        .iter()
        .map(|(t, c)| ((*t).to_string(), (*c).to_string()))
        .collect();

    let tables = conn
        .query("SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'table' AND name NOT LIKE 'sqlite_%'")
        .expect("list tables");

    for table_row in &tables {
        let table = table_row
            .get(0)
            .and_then(beads::storage::SqliteValue::as_text)
            .expect("table name")
            .to_string();
        if table == "issues" {
            continue; // its own `id` column is rewritten directly, not via the list
        }

        let fks = conn
            .query(&format!("PRAGMA foreign_key_list({table})"))
            .expect("foreign key list");
        for fk in &fks {
            // PRAGMA foreign_key_list columns: id, seq, table, from, to, ...
            let referenced = fk.get(2).and_then(beads::storage::SqliteValue::as_text);
            let column = fk.get(3).and_then(beads::storage::SqliteValue::as_text);
            if referenced == Some("issues")
                && let Some(column) = column
            {
                from_schema.insert((table.clone(), column.to_string()));
            }
        }
    }

    let covered: BTreeSet<(String, String)> = ID_BEARING_COLUMNS
        .iter()
        .map(|(t, c)| ((*t).to_string(), (*c).to_string()))
        .collect();

    let missing: Vec<_> = from_schema.difference(&covered).collect();
    assert!(
        missing.is_empty(),
        "these columns hold issue IDs but rename_issue does not rewrite them, so a \
         rename would leave them pointing at a vacated ID: {missing:?}\n\
         Add each pair to ID_BEARING_COLUMNS in src/storage/sqlite.rs."
    );

    let stale: Vec<_> = covered.difference(&from_schema).collect();
    assert!(
        stale.is_empty(),
        "ID_BEARING_COLUMNS names columns that no longer exist in the schema: {stale:?}\n\
         Remove each pair from src/storage/sqlite.rs."
    );
}
```

The `stale` half matters as much as the `missing` half. A dropped table leaves a
`no such table` error at rename time — but only for whoever happens to rename
something next, which could be much later.

title: Resolver fallback for former ids
description: Old IDs resolve to the issue that now holds them. Because the tombstone occupies the old ID, the fix is not a fourth step but a reordering: the two O(1) exact-match steps switch to a live-issue check, a former_ids lookup runs next, and a tombstone-tolerant retry follows so br show on a genuinely deleted issue does not regress to IssueNotFound. All of it sits ahead of the abbreviation scan, which already costs a full SELECT id FROM issues — so the hot path of a fully spelled current ID is untouched. Produces find_id_by_former_id (json_each over the array, excluding tombstones), live_id_exists, and a former_id_fn parameter on IdResolver::resolve_fallible. Consumes former_ids populated by Task 5.
design:
### Task 6: Resolver fallback — old IDs still resolve

`br show bd-p.1` after a rename currently finds the tombstone and reports a
deleted issue. It should find the issue that ID now names.

**The ordering matters and is not obvious.** The tombstone occupies the old ID,
so the exact-match step at `resolve_fallible` step 1 hits it and returns before
any fallback runs. The fix is not to add a fourth step — it is to make the
exact-match steps prefer a *live* issue, and let a tombstone hit fall through:

1. exact match to a **live** issue → return (O(1); the hot path, untouched)
2. prefix-completed exact match to a **live** issue → return (O(1))
3. `former_ids` lookup → return the live issue that used to hold this ID
4. exact match to a **tombstone** → return it, so `br show` on a genuinely

design:
### Task 13: Stop `src/health.rs` implying a `br health` command

This task exists because the confusion actually happened during this project's
own design. `src/health.rs` was read as backing a `br health` command, and the
divergence detector was specced into it before anyone checked. There is no such
command, and that module is the wrong layer for data-level checks.

The module makes this easy to get wrong:

- It is named `health.rs` and sits at the crate root, where every sibling
  (`inheritance.rs`, `close_policy.rs`, `shutdown.rs`) names a *concept*, not a
  command — but "health" is also a plausible command name.
- **It opens at `use std::fmt;` with no `//!` header at all.** Nothing at the top
  of the file says what it is for.
- The explanation that would resolve it — that this is file-state classification
  and that data-level drift is deliberately out of scope — is a `///` comment on
  `AnomalyClass`, forty lines down, where nobody skimming will see it.
- Its only consumer is `src/cli/commands/sync.rs`, so the connection to
  `br sync --status` is invisible from the module itself.

**Files:**
- Modify: `src/health.rs` (add a module doc comment)

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: nothing. Produces nothing. Pure documentation.

- [ ] **Step 1: Read the existing explanation before rewriting it**

```sh
sed -n 30,50p src/health.rs
```

The `AnomalyClass` doc comment already contains the reasoning. The module header
should state the conclusion and leave the reasoning where it is, rather than
duplicating it into two places that can drift apart.

- [ ] **Step 2: Add the module doc comment**

At the very top of `src/health.rs`, before `use std::fmt;`:

```rust
//! Workspace **file-state** classification — is the database readable, is the
//! JSONL intact, are there stale locks or sidecars lying around.
//!
//! **There is no `br health` command, and this module does not back one.** Its
//! only consumer is `src/cli/commands/sync.rs`, which surfaces these anomalies
//! through `br sync --status` (and `--json`, as the `anomalies` array and the
//! `workspace_health` field).
//!
//! The scope is deliberately narrow: this classifies the *files*, never the
//! *data* in them. Drift inside the issue graph — a dotted ID that disagrees
//! with its `parent-child` dep, a stale projection — is not an anomaly here and
//! must not be added. Those belong to `br info --projections`
//! (`src/cli/commands/info.rs`), which reports on graph integrity. The reasoning
//! behind the split is on [`AnomalyClass`] below.
```

Say what it is, say plainly what it is not, and name where the other thing lives.
The negative sentence is the load-bearing one — it is the sentence whose absence
caused the confusion.

- [ ] **Step 3: Check the module name itself is not worth changing**

Renaming to `workspace_health.rs` would be more self-describing, but it touches
seven `crate::health::` paths in `sync.rs` and makes the diff about a rename
rather than about a fix. The doc comment resolves the confusion at the point
where a reader meets it. **Do not rename** unless the reviewer asks — note the
option in the commit body and leave the decision visible.

- [ ] **Step 4: Verify nothing else claims the command exists**

```sh
git grep -n "br health"
```

Expected: only the deliberate "there is no `br health` command" statements in
the epic's stored design. If anything in `docs/`, `README.md` or `skills/`
asserts the command exists, fix it here — that is the whole point of the task.

- [ ] **Step 5: Verify — scoped, NOT the full gate**

```sh
env -u RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN cargo fmt
```

Then re-run the scoped test command from the earlier step of this task. That is
your verification.

**Do not run `task check` here.** It runs clippy over every target and the whole
~3160-test suite, and at two-plus minutes a task it dominates the wall clock of
this plan. The controller runs it at feature boundaries instead. If you believe
this task genuinely needs the full gate — you touched the schema, a shared
trait, or something with blast radius past your own files — say so in your
report and let the controller decide rather than running it yourself.

Doc comments are compiled, and `//!` referencing `[`AnomalyClass`]` must resolve
or the doc build warns. Confirm:

```sh
env -u RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN cargo doc --no-deps 2>&1 | grep -i "warning" | head
```

- [ ] **Step 6: Commit**

```sh
git add src/health.rs .beads/
env -u RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN cargo test --test licensing
git commit -m "docs(health): state that this module does not back a br health command"
```

design:
### Task 14: Give every renamed node its own provenance, not just the top one

**This task exists because of a ruling, not a bug report.** Two briefs in this
epic contradicted each other and the contradiction was resolved in favour of
uniformity.

`rename_issue` currently gives a tombstone and a `former_ids` entry to the
top-level renamed node only. Descendants carried along by the cascade get
neither — their `issues.id` is rewritten and nothing records where they came
from. That was a deliberate choice in the task 5 brief, on the stated grounds
that tombstoning a deep subtree would flood the JSONL. It has two consequences,
both verified live:

- **Old descendant IDs stop resolving.** After `cd-rc6.1` → `cd-trk.1`,
  `br show cd-rc6.1.1` returns `Error: Issue not found`. `find_id_by_former_id`
  (`sqlite.rs:7141`) is an exact `json_each` value match with no prefix
  splicing, so there is nothing for it to find.
- **A stale clone resurrects them on merge.** This is the serious one. The
  tombstone's entire justification is that it propagates the disappearance
  through JSONL so another clone merges a tombstone instead of re-creating a
  live issue. Descendants get no tombstone, so a deep rename is only
  half-propagated — the exact failure the mechanism exists to prevent, one level
  down.

**The ruling:** every renamed node, at any depth, gets the same treatment as the
top-level node. The JSONL cost is proportional to the subtree actually renamed,
which is bounded and rare; the "flooding" concern in the original brief was
speculation, not measurement.

**Files:**
- Modify: `src/storage/sqlite.rs` (`rename_issue_in_tx` and its cascade loop)
- Test: `tests/storage/rename.rs` (append)
- Test: `tests/e2e/reparent.rs` (append — the user-visible half)

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: `insert_rename_tombstone`, `bind_full_issue_insert_params`,
  `FULL_ISSUE_INSERT_SQL`, `descendant_ids` — all already exist
- Produces: no new signature. `rename_issue`'s observable behaviour widens.

- [ ] **Step 1: Read what the top-level node currently gets**

```sh
grep -n "fn rename_issue_in_tx" -A 60 src/storage/sqlite.rs
grep -n "fn insert_rename_tombstone" -A 40 src/storage/sqlite.rs
```

Note three things the existing tombstone path already gets right, because your
per-descendant version must get them right too:

- `external_ref` is set to `None` on the tombstone. `idx_issues_external_ref_unique`
  (`schema.rs:90`) is a partial UNIQUE index with **no status predicate**, so
  tombstones are indexed like live rows. Copying the value would collide with
  the renamed issue that still holds it and fail the whole transaction. A
  descendant with an `external_ref` hits this identically.
- `former_ids` on the tombstone itself is zeroed, so a tombstone cannot hijack a
  `find_id_by_former_id` lookup.
- The row goes in through the shared `FULL_ISSUE_INSERT_SQL` binder, so a future
  column cannot be added to `create_issue` and missed here.

- [ ] **Step 2: Write the failing tests**

Append to `tests/storage/rename.rs`:

```rust
#[test]
fn every_renamed_descendant_records_its_own_former_id() {
    let mut storage = tree();

    storage.rename_issue("bd-p.1", "bd-q.7", "tester").unwrap();

    let grandchild = storage
        .get_issue("bd-q.7.1")
        .unwrap()
        .expect("bd-p.1.1 moved to bd-q.7.1");
    assert_eq!(
        grandchild.former_ids,
        vec!["bd-p.1.1"],
        "a descendant carried by the cascade must record where it came from"
    );
}

#[test]
fn every_vacated_descendant_id_gets_a_tombstone() {
    let mut storage = tree();

    storage.rename_issue("bd-p.1", "bd-q.7", "tester").unwrap();

    let stone = storage
        .get_issue("bd-p.1.1")
        .unwrap()
        .expect("the vacated descendant ID keeps a tombstone");
    assert_eq!(stone.status, Status::Tombstone);
    assert!(
        stone.delete_reason.as_deref().unwrap_or_default().contains("bd-q.7.1"),
        "the tombstone must name where the descendant went; got {:?}",
        stone.delete_reason
    );
}

#[test]
fn a_descendant_old_id_resolves_to_its_new_home() {
    let mut storage = tree();
    storage.rename_issue("bd-p.1", "bd-q.7", "tester").unwrap();

    let found = storage.find_id_by_former_id("bd-p.1.1").unwrap();

    assert_eq!(found.as_deref(), Some("bd-q.7.1"));
}

#[test]
fn descendant_tombstones_do_not_block_the_old_parent_closing() {
    let mut storage = tree();

    storage.rename_issue("bd-p.1", "bd-q.7", "tester").unwrap();
    storage.rename_issue("bd-p.2", "bd-q.8", "tester").unwrap();

    let blockers = storage.get_open_dot_notation_children("bd-p").unwrap();

    assert!(
        blockers.is_empty(),
        "tombstones are terminal and must not count as open children; got {blockers:?}"
    );
}

#[test]
fn a_descendant_carrying_an_external_ref_can_be_renamed() {
    let mut storage = test_db();
    for id in ["bd-x", "bd-x.1", "bd-x.1.1"] {
        let mut issue = fixtures::issue(id);
        issue.id = id.to_string();
        if id == "bd-x.1.1" {
            issue.external_ref = Some("JIRA-777".to_string());
        }
        storage.create_issue(&issue, "tester").unwrap();
    }

    storage
        .rename_issue("bd-x.1", "bd-y.4", "tester")
        .expect("a descendant's external_ref must not collide with its own tombstone");

    let moved = storage.get_issue("bd-y.4.1").unwrap().expect("moved");
    assert_eq!(moved.external_ref.as_deref(), Some("JIRA-777"));
    let stone = storage.get_issue("bd-x.1.1").unwrap().expect("tombstone");
    assert_eq!(stone.external_ref, None, "the tombstone must not hold the reference");
}
```

That last test is the one that will catch the mistake most likely to be made
here. The top-level path already nulls `external_ref`; a per-descendant copy
that forgets to is a transaction-failing bug reachable by any real workspace
that uses external references.

Append to `tests/e2e/reparent.rs` — match that file's existing fixture idiom
rather than inventing one:

- [ ] **Step 3: Run them and confirm they fail**


- [ ] **Step 4: Extend the cascade**

In `rename_issue_in_tx`, the descendant loop currently calls

records the top-level node gets: append its old ID to its own `former_ids`, and

Keep the ordering that already works — descendants deepest-first, then the node

- [ ] **Step 5: Check the JSONL cost is what you expect**

title: br detach is the one mutating command that will operate on a tombstone
description: Symptom: get_issue_from_conn is 'WHERE id = ?' with no status predicate (sqlite.rs:3920-3932), id_exists delegates to it, rename_issue guards only on existence (7584-7595), and detach_one never checks Status::Tombstone — while remove_dependency, label, comment and status paths all go through ensure_issue_mutable_in_tx ('cannot ... tombstone issue'). WHERE id IN (...) per chunk and only genuinely future-dated rows fall back to a statement each; SQL MAX() was rejected because it yields equality, which determine_action treats as Skip. title: find_id_by_former_id gives nondeterministic answers on a former-id collision
description: Standalone follow-up from the bds-a23 final review, deliberately not parented to that epic (it concerns resolver determinism, not the hierarchy invariant). find_id_by_former_id uses LIMIT 1 with no ORDER BY (src/storage/sqlite.rs), and the JSONL-materialized path at show.rs:966 uses HashMap::values().find_map, whose iteration order is randomized per process. So on a collision the two paths can disagree with each other, and the JSONL path can give DIFFERENT ANSWERS ON DIFFERENT RUNS of the same command against the same file. A collision needs two live issues claiming one former id, unreachable through rename_issue alone (the tombstone holds the primary key) but reachable through a JSONL merge of divergent branches. Fix: ORDER BY i.id LIMIT 1 in the SQL, min_by_key in the mirror — making both deterministic and identical.
close_reason: fixed: ORDER BY i.id in the SQL, min over live rows in the JSONL mirror, and the hash-match mirror sorted to match
